prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Not every man knows what he shall sing at the end, Watching the pier as the ship sails away, or what it will seem like When he’s held by the sea’s roar, motionless, there at the end, Or what he shall hope for once it is clear that he’ll never go back. When the time has passed to prune the rose or caress the cat, When the sunset torching the lawn and the full moon icing it down No longer appear, not every man knows what he’ll discover instead. When the weight of the past leans against nothing, and the sky Is no more than remembered light, and the stories of cirrus And cumulus come to a close, and all the birds are suspended in flight, Not every man knows what is waiting for him, or what he shall sing When the ship he is on slips into darkness, there at the end.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Not, Watching, When

outputs.L1:
Not every man knows what he shall sing at the end,
Watching the pier recede as the ship sails away, or what it will feel like
When he is held by the sea's roar, motionless, there at the end,
Or what he shall hope for once it is clear he will never return.
When the hour has passed for pruning roses or caressing the cat,
When the sunset that sets the lawn ablaze and the full moon that glazes it in frost
No longer appear, not every man knows what he will find in their place.
When the weight of the past leans upon nothing, and the sky
Is no more than remembered light, and the tales told by cirrus
And cumulus draw to a close, and all the birds hang suspended in flight,
Not every man knows what awaits him, or what he shall sing
When the ship he is on slips into darkness, there at the end.
outputs.L2: No one can say for certain what song will rise to his lips in that final hour, gazing back at the shore as the vessel carries him away, or how it will feel to be swallowed by the ocean's thunder, still and unmoving, at journey's end. Nor can he guess what he'll long for once the truth sinks in—that return is no longer possible. When the season for trimming roses or stroking a cat's fur has passed, when neither the sunset setting the grass ablaze nor the full moon frosting it silver appears any longer, no man can be sure what will fill that void. When the burden of yesterday rests on nothing at all, when the sky becomes merely a memory of brightness, when the tales told by wispy cirrus and towering cumulus clouds reach their final page, and every bird hangs frozen mid-flight, no one truly knows what awaits him, or what melody he'll sing as his ship dissolves into the shadows, there at the very end.
outputs.L3:
# On the Threshold of Departure

Not every man knows what he will sing at the moment of death, nor what he will feel as that final hour approaches—that quiet, inevitable moment symbolized so completely by standing at the pier's edge, watching a ship slip away toward the horizon, growing smaller until it disappears into the grey distance where sea meets sky. We imagine, perhaps, that we will know what to say, what to feel, what words might rise to meet that ultimate silence. But the truth is far less certain, far more humbling than we allow ourselves to believe.

There is a profound uncertainty in contemplating what one will hope for in that final reckoning—once it becomes unmistakably clear that there is no return, no second passage back across the water to the world of the living. What does a person yearn for when yearning itself becomes futile? Does the mind reach backward toward regret, or does it release, finally, into acceptance? No one can say with certainty until they stand at that particular shore.

The poem turns its gaze toward the endings of small, simple pleasures—the kind we rarely notice until their absence looms before us. The careful pruning of roses in a quiet garden, the soft warmth of a cat's fur beneath an affectionate hand, the daily miracle of sunset bleeding into evening, the pale wash of moonlight across a familiar windowsill. These are the modest joys that compose a life, and it is precisely their loss—their quiet cessation—that weighs most heavily when death draws near. Not grand achievements or dramatic sorrows, but these small, tender rituals we too often take for granted.

As death approaches, the past begins to lose its weight and substance. What once seemed permanent—memory, history, the accumulated years—grows thin and insubstantial, like mist burning off in early light. The sky itself, once a canopy of endless possibility, becomes merely a memory, a recollection of something once witnessed rather than something still experienced. The ongoing narratives of the natural world—the drifting clouds, the calling birds, the whole unfolding drama of existence—slow, and slow again, until they arrive at a stillness that feels less like ending and more like a held breath.

And so we are left with this essential truth: no one truly knows what awaits them beyond that threshold, nor what final words or songs might rise unbidden from the depths of the self in that last moment. We remain, all of us, passengers unaware of our own destination, watching as our ship—laden with all we have been and all we might have said—slips quietly into the gathering darkness, carrying with it questions that will only be answered, if they are answered at all, on the other side of that silent water.
outputs.L4:
# The Unmoored Ship

There is a ship that waits beyond the bay,
Its sails half-furled against the fading light,
And no man knows the hour of its sway,
Nor what dark waters wait beyond his sight.

He stands upon the shore of one last hour,
His feet still rooted in the shifting sand,
And feels within him life's diminishing power,
Yet cannot grasp what he shall understand.

What word will rise up from his failing breath?
What final thought will linger, incomplete?
No man has charted still the coast of death,
No compass guides him toward that far retreat.

The rose that bloomed so red at morning's start
Now bends its head, petals drift and fall—
Each crimson piece a fragment of the heart
That knew not when the darkness came to call.

The sunset burns its brief and dying gold
Across a sky that soon will turn to gray,
A beauty that no living hand can hold,
A fire that gutters into fading day.

The moon ascends where once the sun held reign,
Pale witness to the turning of the earth,
Its borrowed light a soft and silver skein
That speaks not of an ending, nor a birth.

The clouds drift on in shapes that will not last,
Dissolving into vapor, into air—
Each formless thing a shadow of the past,
A wisp of what was never truly there.

And birds hang suspended, wings spread wide,
Caught in that moment just before the fall,
Not knowing if the wind will be their guide
Or if the earth will claim them, one and all.

So too the man who faces his last light,
Uncertain of the shore he travels toward,
Whether peace or darkness, day or night,
Awaits him past that unfamiliar ford.

The ship sails on. No hand can stay its course.
No voice can call it back from where it's bound.
We watch it vanish with a quiet force,
Into the silence where no shore is found.

And we who watch from windows, we who wait,
Who tend our roses, watch our sunsets fade,
We too shall meet that same unknown strait,
Not knowing what final word will be said.

What shall we speak when shadows dim our eyes?
What final breath, what whisper, what last sound?
We do not know—beneath the fading skies,
We are all voyagers to that same unbound ground.

The bird still hovers, wings against the wind,
The cloud still drifts, uncertain where it goes,
The moon still rises where the day has thinned,
And no one living yet the answer knows.

So let the ship sail on toward what it seeks,
Let rose and sunset teach us, without pride,
That mystery is the language death still speaks,
And every soul must sail that final tide.
outputs.L5:
# When No One Is Watching

Character is often defined not by what we do in public, but by what we do in private. It's easy to be kind, honest, and disciplined when others are observing us—when our actions are subject to judgment, praise, or criticism. The real test comes in the quiet moments, when there is no audience, no accountability, and no one keeping score.

Think about the small choices that make up daily life: picking up litter that isn't yours, being honest on a form no one will check, or resisting the urge to cut corners on a task no one will inspect closely. These moments reveal something deeper than performance—they reveal values.

Watching ourselves, ironically, can be one of the hardest habits to cultivate. Self-awareness in the absence of external observation requires a kind of internal compass, a commitment to principles that doesn't waver based on whether someone might notice. This is often what separates genuine integrity from mere image management.

There's a quiet strength in choosing to act rightly not because we fear being caught, but because we've decided that certain standards matter to us regardless of circumstance. When we align our private actions with our stated values, we build a kind of internal consistency that fosters trust—not just with others, but with ourselves.

In a world increasingly filled with cameras, social media, and constant connectivity, it's rare to find moments of true privacy. But it's precisely in those rare moments—when we believe we're unwatched—that our truest selves emerge. Perhaps character isn't about grand gestures made in the spotlight, but about the accumulation of small, unnoticed choices that shape who we are when it seems like nobody's looking.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the style of Mark Strand about facing the end of life, using recurring images of a ship sailing away and the phrase "not every man knows."
counterfactuals.output:
**Not Every Man Knows**

There is a harbor in me
where a ship keeps loosening its ropes,
and I stand on the dock of myself
watching the water widen.

Not every man knows
the moment the ship stops being his,
how the white sail turns
into a small fact on the horizon,
then into nothing, then into the horizon itself.

I have practiced disappearing
by watching other things disappear.
The ship does this so well
I sometimes think it is teaching me,
patient as a father who already knows
the son will not follow.

Not every man knows
that the sea keeps no record,
that the wake behind a ship
is only the water forgetting
what passed through it.

I fold my hands the way the dead do,
though I am not yet finished
with this business of watching.
The ship, small as a comma now,
edits me out of its long sentence.

Some nights I am the harbor.
Some nights I am the thing leaving.
Not every man knows
which one he is
until the light goes,
until the water is only water,
until there is nothing on it at all
to prove a ship was ever there,

and even the harbor,
patient, empty, ringed with lamps,
begins to look like something
that was never waiting
for anything to return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a meditative poem about mortality that repeats the line "there at the end" and explores what a person might sing or feel as death approaches.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains

There at the end, the light comes soft and low,
like afternoon forgetting how to burn,
and what I thought I'd say, I do not know—
the words I saved dissolve at every turn.

There at the end, perhaps I'll hum a tune
my mother sang while hanging clothes to dry,
some fragment of a half-remembered noon,
too small to be a prayer, too true to die.

I thought I'd feel the weight of all my sins,
the ledger closing, judgment drawing near—
instead there's just the wind against my skin,
the strange relief of no more need for fear.

There at the end, will I regret the years
I spent afraid of exactly this?
Or will I find that even here, tears
are just another form that love takes, still, in this—

this room, this bed, this narrowing of sight,
where someone's hand will hold my hand, and stay,
and I'll stop measuring the dark from light
and simply rest inside the fading day.

There at the end, no answer, no great sound,
no trumpet-call to prove the soul was right—
just breath grown thin, the way a year turns round,
just letting go the way a bird takes flight

without a plan, without a chart to steer,
just wing and wind and sky and then—release.
There at the end, perhaps I'll lose my fear
the way a wave dissolves in perfect peace,

still singing something wordless, low and slow,
a sound I've always known but couldn't place,
there at the end, when everything I know
becomes the light, becomes the falling grace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a lyrical poem, similar to Mark Strand's "The End," reflecting on uncertainty, memory, and the moment when life quietly slips away?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Light

Not everyone knows what they will lose
when the evening finally arrives,
the porch light dimming into blue,
the names of things beginning to slide

from their places, quietly, like guests
who leave before the party's done.
Not everyone knows which small request
will be the last, which rising sun

they'll fail to see as morning, only light,
undifferentiated, gray.
We move through rooms we knew by heart at night
and find the furniture has changed its way

of being furniture. The clock still ticks
but time forgets to listen now.
Someone is calling from the far edge, thick
with static, and we can't recall just how

we knew that voice, though once it was
the only sound that mattered, once
it called us home through fields, through doors,
through years we wore like ordinary clothes.

Not everyone knows the hour when the mind
lets go of what it cannot hold—
the birthday, the address, the kind
of bird that used to sing before the cold—

and what remains is something else: a hush,
a shape where memory had been,
the way a river, after rush
and rapids, meets the sea and enters in

without a splash, without a sound
we'd recognize as ending. Just this: 
the self dissolving, unbound,
into whatever comes after this.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem using nature imagery—sunsets, roses, clouds, birds—to symbolize the fading of a life, ending with the image of a ship disappearing into darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Horizon

The sunset bleeds its final gold
across a sky grown thin and old,
while roses, heavy on the vine,
let fall their petals, one by one, in time.

The clouds that once raced wild and free
now drift like whispers toward the sea,
their edges soft, their colors spent,
dissolving into firmament.

A bird calls out—one last refrain—
then folds its wings against the rain,
and settles where the branches bow,
its song grown quiet, softer now.

The garden dims. The light grows thin.
The day exhales, and night steps in.
What bloomed so bright, so fierce, so brave,
surrenders gently to the wave.

And there, upon the darkening tide,
a ship sails on, alone, wide-eyed,
its sails still catching one last beam
before it fades into the dream.

No cry, no struggle, no goodbye—
just distance widening 'neath the sky,
until the hull, the mast, the light
are swallowed whole by patient night.

The water closes, smooth and deep,
where ship and shadow now both sleep,
and all that's left upon the shore
is silence... and the waves' soft roar.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a somber, reflective poem about not knowing what awaits after death, blending images of the sea, the sky, and the passage of time.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Tide Does Not Say**

I have watched the horizon long enough
to know it keeps its secrets well—
that line where water learns to be sky,
where sky forgets it was ever water,
and neither one will tell me what comes after.

The gulls repeat their single question
into wind that carries it nowhere.
The waves arrive already leaving,
each one a small rehearsal
for the last unraveling.

I think of all the ships that font
folded into fog and never wrote back,
how the sea keeps no address
for where the going goes.
Only this: the tide returns,
though never with the same water,
never with the answer.

Time moves like light across December water—
thin, indifferent, unable to warm
what it touches.
I have asked the dusk so many times
what waits beyond the dark it drapes each evening,
and each night it only dims the question further,
pulls the stars up like small witnesses
who also do not know, who also
flicker and are still.

Perhaps the not-knowing is the vigil—
the standing at the edge of every evening,
salt-air and grey light,
holding what cannot be held,
watching what cannot be seen
arrive the way all horizons arrive:
by disappearing
the moment we approach.

I will not pretend to comfort.
I will only say: the sea keeps moving
without needing to know its shore.
The sky keeps darkening
without apology.
And I keep standing here,
small before the unanswered vastness,
learning to let the waiting
be its own kind of peace.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
